title: Smartphone Specs Explained: What the Numbers Mean
description: Plain-language explanations of smartphone specs - display nits, battery mAh, chipsets, camera sensors, RAM and storage - and what matters.
content:
Spec sheets are dense with numbers that sound meaningful and only some of which are. This guide explains the core smartphone specifications in plain language, with an eye on what actually changes day-to-day experience.

## Display

**Resolution** is the pixel count — higher means sharper text and images, but past roughly 400 pixels-per-inch the difference is invisible at normal viewing distance. **Refresh rate** (60Hz, 90Hz, 120Hz) is how many times the image updates per second: higher is smoother in scrolling and animation, and the jump from 60 to 90 is more noticeable than from 90 to 120. **Brightness in nits** measures luminance: anything above roughly 1000 sustained nits handles outdoor shade well; peak-nit figures (often 2000+) are achieved on small screen areas for short periods, so compare sustained values where available. Panel type (OLED, LTPO) affects contrast and battery behaviour: OLED gives true blacks, LTPO lets the refresh rate drop to save power.

## Battery

**Capacity in mAh** is energy storage — but endurance depends on capacity divided by consumption, so a smaller battery with an efficient chip can outlast a larger one with a hungry chip. Compare capacity within similar phone sizes and processor classes only. **Charging speed in watts** is the ceiling the phone accepts; the charger in the box (if any) is a separate question. **Wireless charging wattage** is typically below wired speed, and some phones omit wireless charging entirely.

## Performance silicon

**Chipset** (A-series, Snapdragon, Tensor, Dimensity) determines CPU/GPU class and modem generation. Marketing names matter less than generation: a current mid-range chip often beats a flagship from three generations back. **RAM** supports multitasking — 6–8GB is comfortable for normal use, more matters mainly for heavy games and long app retention. **Storage** is both capacity and speed: the read/write technology (UFS versions on Android) affects app-install and load times, while capacity determines how much you can keep before the phone starts nagging.

## Cameras

**Sensor size** is the strongest single predictor of photo quality: a larger sensor gathers more light, improving low-light performance. **Megapixels** determine detail ceiling and cropping latitude; beyond ~50MP on a phone sensor, extra pixels usually mean pixel-binning rather than resolving more real detail. **Aperture (f-number)** controls light intake and depth of field — lower f-numbers admit more light. **Telephoto reach** (optical zoom) is the difference between cropping and actually zooming; a dedicated telephoto lens beats digital zoom every time. **Video capability** should be checked for stabilization per lens, not just resolution on the spec line.

## Connectivity

**5G** requires both modem support and the right bands for your carrier — the logo alone does not guarantee usable 5G. **Wi-Fi generation** (Wi-Fi 6, 6E, 7) affects speed and congestion handling on compatible routers; upgrade value depends on your router, not the phone. **NFC** enables contactless payments and quick pairing. **Bluetooth version** affects range and efficiency; most users will not notice version differences with modern headphones. **USB-C** is the connector, but supported standards vary — check whether the port carries data at USB 2.0 or higher speeds.

## What to ignore

Marketing AI labels without a feature list you can verify, pixel counts above print needs, peak-brightness wars, and any benchmark number tested under conditions you cannot replicate. When a field is missing from the sheet, it is unknown — record it as such instead of assuming the worst or the best.

## Cameras: what the numbers hide

**Megapixels** count pixels, not detail. A 50MP main sensor binned to 12MP output often produces cleaner photos than a 108MP sensor with the same pixel size, because binning averages noise away. What matters more: sensor physical size (larger gathers more light), aperture (lower f-number passes more light), and whether optical stabilisation is present — OIS corrects hand shake at shutter speeds where unsteady hands would otherwise blur the frame.

**Optical vs digital zoom.** Optical zoom moves real glass, so detail survives. Digital zoom crops and upscales; the number in the zoom label (10×, 30×, 100×) describes magnification, not resolution. When a phone lists both, compare the optical figure first — it is the honest ceiling for sharp detail.

**Video resolution and frame rate.** 4K at 60fps stores four times the pixels of 1080p at 30fps and fills storage correspondingly. Check which lens records at the top rate: many phones record 4K60 on the main camera only, with ultrawide and telephoto capped lower.

## Software and support windows

**OS update commitment** is the number of major Android or iOS versions a vendor promises. **Security patch commitment** is how long critical fixes keep arriving. They are separate promises — a phone can receive security patches after the last OS upgrade. Compare both numbers across brands; a longer window keeps the device usable and bank-app compatible for more years.

**AI feature lists** on spec sheets mix on-device and cloud features. On-device features work offline and keep data local; cloud features need a connection and may change or be withdrawn when the server-side model changes. Treat the list as a capability inventory, not a permanent guarantee.

## How to use this page with our database

Every product page on CompareForge shows the same fields side by side with a median of our own published records — not a market survey. A figure above the median is not automatically better: a heavier phone often carries a larger battery. Use the median table to see where a model sits among the phones we track, then open a side-by-side comparison to see the differences that matter for your use case.
